passages.original: Igitur non omitlens priscos illos communesque cum omnibus gentibus errores, quibus ante adventum Christi in carne omne humanum genus obligabatur astrictum, nec enumerans patriæ portenta ipsa diabolica, pene numero vincentia Ægyptiaca d (quorum nonnulla, Ji- neamentis adhuc deformibus intra vel extra deserta moenia solito more rigentia, torvis vultibus intuemur), neque nominatim inclamitans montes ipsos aut colles vel fluvios olim exitiales, nunc vero humanis usibus utiles, quibus divinus honor a caeco tunc populo cumulabatur ; et tacens vetustos immanium tyrannorum annos qui in aliis longe positis regionibus vulgati sunt ( ita ut Porphyrius rabidus canis orientalis adversus Ecclesiam e, dementiæ suae ac vanitatis stylo hoc etiam annecteret: Britannia est f, inquiens, fertilis prorincia tyrannorum), illa tamen proferre conabor in- medium quae temporibus imperatorum Romanorum et passa est, et aliis intulit civibus longe positis a mala ;
passages.english: Therefore, not leaving aside those ancient errors common to all nations, by which, before the coming of Christ in the flesh, the whole human race was held bound and constrained, nor enumerating the diabolical monstrosities of [our] homeland itself, almost surpassing in number those of Egypt (some of which we still behold, with their features yet misshapen, stiff in their accustomed manner within or outside the deserted walls, with grim faces), nor calling out by name the very mountains or hills or rivers, once deadly, but now useful for human needs, on which divine honour was then heaped by a blind people; and passing over in silence the ancient years of monstrous tyrants, which have been spread abroad in other far-distant regions (so that Porphyry, the rabid eastern dog against the Church, added this too with the pen of his madness and vanity: "Britain," he says, "is a province fertile in tyrants"), I shall nevertheless try to bring into the open those evils which [Britain] both suffered in the times of the Roman emperors and inflicted on other citizens far distant;
passages.notes: The work label combines Gildas' De Excidio Britanniae with the unrelated comedy Querolus; the passage is from Gildas, De Excidio 4. Stray letters (d, e, f, a) are footnote marks and have been omitted. Scanning errors corrected: 'omitlens' read as omittens, 'Ji- neamentis' as lineamentis, 'prorincia' as provincia, 'in- medium' as in medium. The sentence is unfinished and continues in the following passage. The famous saying 'Britain is a province fertile in tyrants' is attributed by Gildas to Porphyry, though it is usually traced to Jerome, who quotes it from Porphyry.
